idiom_name: mixin functions composed onto one class (extends any constructor) instead of two linked objects
implementation_notes: An object has exactly one prototype chain, so the twin's two-class structure would require two instances that reference each other; the local idiom is composition onto one object. MDN states it directly: 'A class can only have a single superclass, so multiple inheritance from tooling classes, for example, is not possible. The functionality must be provided by the superclass', and the same page shows the mixin form - a function taking a superclass and returning a subclass that extends it (class Bar extends calculator(randomizer(Foo)) {}); Object.assign covers the constructor-less case by copying own enumerable properties onto a prototype. What still needs the twin shape: two parents that each own state and a constructor (a mixin cannot usefully run two constructors), or two subsystems that each require their own addressable object - there, link two objects explicitly and remove any listener or timer that holds one end, because nothing else will release the pair.
pitfalls: Mixins are applied at class-definition time, so private fields (#x) colliding across two mixins are a syntax error, and instanceof no longer reflects the composition - MDN notes a mixin-composed class is not a subclass of its mixins, so brand checks must be structural or use Symbol.hasInstance.
Object.assign copies own enumerable properties only: getters, non-enumerable members and prototype methods are not merged, so it merges data rather than behaviour.
Reassigning a prototype chain with Object.setPrototypeOf to add a second parent is discouraged by MDN and deoptimises engines; class expressions in extends are the supported composition path.
Two mutually referencing objects are ordinary collectable cycles in JavaScript, but an event listener, timer or framework registry that holds one end keeps the whole pair alive until it is removed.
